utterances.text: Yes. General Galevski, why did Mr. Boskoski hold these regular meetings of the collegium; do you know?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably he thought this was the best for the work of the ministry, to have all highest-ranking officials who would exchange among each others, report each one on the area they cover, and to coordinate their joint work on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that Minister Boskoski regularly convened these meetings. How often during the crisis time of summer 2001 would Mr. Boskoski convene such meetings? Daily, weekly, more than once a day?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was not a precise pattern. Sometimes it was in one day or two days but at least there was one meeting per week and this depended also on the situation and on the problems on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sure. That makes sense. So during times of particular tension when there was heavy fighting on the ground and soldiers or police officers were killed, would the collegium be convened more frequently?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to precisely say in what kind of situation. I know that we were very often in the cabinet of the minister where these collegiums were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday at page 3742 of the transcript you explained how in June of 2001 the public in Macedonia was very disturbed when they heard that the police and the army were withdrawing from Aracinovo. Do you remember explaining that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So both police and army units participated in the fighting at Aracinovo.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You explained yesterday at page 3742 of the transcript that you received personally from Minister Boskoski "the order to withdraw from Aracinovo." Now, just to be clear, that order from Minister Boskoski only applied to the withdrawal of police units; correct?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The minister issued to me that task but maybe it was not noted exactly not to withdraw from the ground but to stop with these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after that order was issued by the Minister Boskoski, were the activities of the police at Aracinovo stopped?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday at page 3750 of the transcript you also explained that during joint combat operations carried out by the police and army in 2001, "the question remained open, who is superior to whom, or who commands to whom?" Do you remember explaining that to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said it as I will repeat it now. There was a dilemma within the state leadership while us with the defence leadership, we didn't have any problem and we were not burdened by who was in charge of what. We just were interested in conducting our work professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So -- but in a practical sense, during those joint operations, police commanders retained some level of command authority over the police officers in their units.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you. Who were the ones that had command authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So during those joint operations in which both army units and police units were involved, police commanders, commanders of the police units, retained some level of command authority over the police officers in their units.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For example, police commanders operating in those joint operations could still discipline their subordinates for infractions or misconduct. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On Tuesday, you explained how in 2001, and still today, if the minister of the interior was not satisfied with the performance of a police officer, the minister could transfer that police officer to a different position. This was at page 3678 of the transcript. Do you recall explaining this to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure whether it was explained exactly that way. The minister had the right to transfer a police officer to some other position, but not those police officers -- lower-ranking of the police officers. More of the higher-ranking police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you also explained that punishment of police -- punishment of a police officer by the minister can only occur after the completion of a disciplinary procedure carried out by the permanent committee within the Ministry of Interior that addresses disciplinary matters. Do you recall that? Do you recall explaining this to my colleague?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The minister can confirm the proposal of the disciplinary committee or possibly to recheck it. So he has a right to correct the proposed measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come to that in a minute. And in 2001, that permanent committee for disciplinary matters reported to the minister, right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the minister who makes decision to establish such a committee. Therefore, this disciplinary committee, of course, reports to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can please show what is 65 ter 379, please. And while we're waiting for it to come up, I have a document, a one-page document, and perhaps if the court usher could provide the parties and the Judges and the witness with a copy, and perhaps a copy could be placed on the ELMO. Your Honours, what you see on your screen is page 1 of the collective agreement of the Ministry of Interior. And the Prosecution does not have a full Macedonian version and that's why I've simply distributed this one page because there is one particular Article I would like to explore with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, witness, if you could -- first of all, if we could move to the -- yep, that is correct ask the correct page, thank you. Witness, if you could take a look at that page that has been put next to you - I don't know if you need your glasses. Mr. Usher, perhaps you can turn that page around so the witness can see it. I'd like, General Galevski, if you could read to us what the text of Article 149 says. It's the Article at the top of the page. But I'd like you to read -- I'd like you to read it in Macedonian, please, General. That's why you need to look at the hard copy that I've given you. General? General -- general, can ask you something?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see also on the screen. Okay, Article 149.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you looking at the Macedonian version?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the screen, on the left side I have it in Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can you read what Article 149 says.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "If the minister does not agree with the proposal he can return the case to a review if the factual situation is wrongly or insufficiently viewed or some normative provision is wrongly implemented or may bring different decision or this -- can be brought according to Article 139 of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So Article 149 of the collective agreement confirms what you told us before, that it is the minister of the interior who to this day has the last word about whether to discipline someone or how to discipline someone within the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would mark this collective agreement for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P382, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you explained yesterday at page 3678 of the transcript that the committee investigating the role of the forces of the Ministry of Interior who participated in the events in Ljuboten in 2001 did not receive the name or names of any police officers who might have committed misconduct. Do you recall explaining that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Suppose Minister Boskoski had received a name of a police officer who allegedly committed misconduct in Ljuboten village, if Minister Boskoski had received such information, it was within his powers to transfer that police officer to another position or to ask the superior of that police officer to present a report to the disciplinary commission?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we object to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, we didn't get the last part, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We object this way of questioning, and we think that these assumptions are not based on the testimony of the witness and they are speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to clarify the information provided to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Suppose the minister had received the name or names of police officers who committed misconduct in Ljuboten village back in August/September 2001. What powers would the minister have had at his disposal?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would not fire him immediately. He has on his disposal the given bodies that would make -- reflect -- that would submit a report to the minister and that would make him report -- reflect on what further measures he would undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So the minister had the authority if such a situation arose to instruct his subordinates to submit a report about the person involved?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me be more precise. This unit for internal control and professional standards is directly related to the minister and it helps the minister to check certain information he gets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, this -- this institution was mentioned even before at the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. In 2001, if Minister Boskoski had received such information, a name or names of certain police officers, could the minister also have directed the superior of that police officer, for example, perhaps the head of the criminal police or the head of a police station, to obtain relevant facts and provide the information to the disciplinary committee or the -- the unit for internal control?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister would do this, but not with commander of the station but with his most immediate advisors, the people most immediate subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then the immediate subordinates of the minister would have the duty to pass those instructions down the chain of command to the appropriate persons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the -- in the interior ministry there is a clear hierarchy which is very much respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the persons then who received these instructions lower down on the chain of command would then have the duty to obtain the relevant information and report it back up through the chain of command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They should report back up through an Official Note, but the situation, regardless of whether the findings are positive or negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that -- these procedures, these -- these procedures were functioning as well in 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they did, but in a very difficult manner, because most of the people employed in the police were at the check-points and did not really have the chance to make some misconduct because they were permanently under the control of the -- of a superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. General, do you agree that sometimes, even commanders, even superior officers make mistakes?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is human to make mistakes and I do not exclude the possibility for anyone to make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 2001, what was the procedure within the Ministry of the Interior when a superior breached his duty or superior or a police commander to provide all of the relevant facts about possible police misconduct up the chain of command or to the disciplinary committee or to the unit for internal control? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regulations are varied for everyone, regardless of where a person is positioned in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there may be a problem either with the translation or with the transcript. The response in the English transcript says: "The regulations are varied for everyone."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ah. The regulations are valid for everyone, all right. Well, then, understandably the regulations apply to everyone. But suppose -- what would happen when a superior made a mistake or breached his duty and did not provide all of the relevant information up the chain of command; in other words, when a superior did not adhere to the regulations, what would happen then?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat again. The regulations related to disciplinary responsibility are valid for all and apply to all. The higher the employee is positioned, the lesser is the possibility for him to be involved in this breach of regulations. This is the reason why most often such a cases, not only during the time of Minister Boskoski but also before him and after him, were transferred to other positions as a measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that you've answered my question, General. I think my question was reasonably clear. What I need to know is, what would happen if a superior - could be a police commander, a commander of a police station, could be a squad leader, could be someone in between or someone higher - what would happen if such a person did not fulfil his duty to provide all relevant information up the chain of command or to the disciplinary committee? Would anything happen?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the whole -- this is the third or fourth time I will be repeating. This is something to be dealt by this unit for internal control. So this unit is in charge of the whole matter. They are the ones t hat have to establish whether the commander, as you said, has shown misconduct and is -- or is in breach of duty and it is this unit that proposes measures against him, starting with disciplinary and there could be even a criminal report, if the case is such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you aware of any such proceedings that were started by the unit for internal control during 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the time my colleague the deputy minister that was in charge after that unit, his name was Slavko. I used to meet him very often as he was going to the minister's office. This -- the very fact that I met him there made me think that he was often engaged in such matters. I do not know what cases he was involved in. He was not supposed to inform me anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So then, General, we can take -- we can take it, then, that the answer to my question, my last question, is no.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether concrete checkups were made. There were activities that were undertaken but I couldn't say on what cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. On Tuesday at page 3648 of the transcript, you agreed with the proposition put to you by my colleague that it is not the competence of the minister of the interior to "operatively carry out tasks nor to effectively control the police officers in the field." Do you remember explaining this?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Who this refers to? Who are those that do not have the right to do this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe my question was unclear. My colleague put to you a proposition that the minister of the interior, minister himself, does not carry out operative tasks in the field nor does the minister effectively control the police officers in the field. And you agreed that that was a correct proposition.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then yesterday at page 3718 of the transcript you also agreed with the proposition put to you by Ms. Residovic that just because a person receives a uniform from the police and a weapon from the police, that does not mean that the person becomes a police reservist under the effective control of the ministry. Do you remember that you agreed with that proposition as well?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is a part of what I said. In order to be a member of the police in addition to possessing uniform and weapons the person should go through a checkup, examinations, to check his health background and then to be assigned -- to be issued an identification card. This is -- this all is a set of things that make a person a police officer. Only the uniform and the weapon are not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. General, can you define the concept of effective control for us, please.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, the term "effective control" is not very clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yesterday at pages 3712 to 3714 of the transcript my colleague asked you some questions about the two committees that the Ministry of Interior established to look into the events in Ljuboten. One committee established by Minister Boskoski in August 2001; and the second committee established by Minister Kostov in March of 2003. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you agreed with a proposition expressed by Ms. Residovic that the tasks, circumstances, and possibilities of the two committees were completely different. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. With respect to the committee that was established by Ljube Boskoski in August of 2001, you explained that the members of the committee were the most responsible officers of the Ministry of the Interior at that time. And you explained that therefore each of those high-ranking officers, one of them, of course, was you, could use his own line of command to ensure that the Ministry of the Interior investigated the events in Ljuboten efficiently. Do you recall explaining that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the person at the top of those lines of command was the minister, Mr. Boskoski, is that right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we -- perhaps with the assistance of the court usher can we provide the binder of our exhibits to General Galevski again, please. And if we could see Exhibit P00073 on the screen. It is in tab 2 of the Prosecution's binder, Your Honours. I may have misspoke. I'm sorry, it's tab 1 of the Prosecution's binder, Your Honours. And if the usher could assist General Galevski by turning to the Macedonian original version of what is in tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have the Macedonian version in front of you, General Galevski?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention, please, to part II. And in the middle of part II it says this: "The commission, from item 1 of this decision, has the task to review the circumstances and analyse the activities undertaken by the security forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to repel the armed attacks of terrorist groups on 12 August 2001 in the village of Ljuboten, Skopje." Are you following with me?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that to review the circumstances and analyse the activities of those security forces, to do that, first, you would need to know the composition of the unit or units from the Ministry of the Interior that took part in the activities in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you would also want to know the capacity or capacities of the unit or units of the Ministry of Internal Affairs that operated in Ljuboten. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are schedules and lists for all the deployed persons up until the last participant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Hmm. And can you tell us, please, where we would find the schedules and lists for all the employees of the Ministry of the Interior who participated in the events in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the area of Ljuboten, since -- until Goran Georgievski got the task from me to engage the posebna unit, active and reserve police forces were engaged only from the territory of OVR Cair, meaning that this information are found in OVR Cair, that is in the police stations of Butel and Mirkovci on which territory the village of Ljuboten is, while about the composition of the posebna units that I sent, there is still a posebna, a Special Unit sector in the MVR so I think that this is the place where you can find the entire lists of the police officers who were participating in the serving as a live shield between the villages of Ljuboten and the other residents of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can we turn please -- moving back to part II of the decision, if we can turn now to part III. It says: "The commission is obliged immediately to start carrying out the tasks determined in item II and to prepare a report about the determined facts, with an opinion about the grounds, justification and regularity of the activities undertaken by the security forces of the Ministry." Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So to prepare such an opinion regarding the activities, the regularity of the activities of the security forces who were operating in Ljuboten, you would need to analyse how the legal powers, the lawful powers of that unit, were exercised, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn now, Your Honours, to what is in tab 3 of your binders. This is marked for identification P379.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn to tab 3, please, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And perhaps if the usher to help the General, because we need to turn to what is ERN N000-8907 which is up in the upper right-hand corner, hopefully. It's about the fourth page in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you'll see that this is the decision from then minister Hari Kostov to establish a second commission to look into the events in Ljuboten. This is the decision of 7 March 2003. Could you turn to what is the top of page 2 in the English but it's part II so it may be on the first page of the Macedonian version. Part II begins with the words "the commission referred to in part I." Do you see that general?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "The commission referred to in part I of this decision shall have the task to investigate and analyse all materials and documents relating to the events which took place in the territory of Ljuboten, Skopje, in August 2001, ascertain the composition and capacity of the unit which took action in this period, including the identity of each of its members individually, establish the causes and circumstances surrounding the deaths of the victims." And then in the last two lines: "Investigate how the legal powers of the unit were exercised." Are you following me, General?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you agree, then, that the tasks of the two committees were actually quite similar?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Tell me, General Galevski, could both committees have spoken with one or more of the Ljuboten residents who had been detained on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know when they have conversed but I would most responsibly say that in 2003 as a free citizen I was able to go in Ljuboten and talk to anyone, while in 2001 that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 2001, could you go to Skopje city hospital?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally not, because if someone is to go there is the inspectors of that police station that are covering this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, General, you were the head of the uniformed police division, you're telling us today that in 2001 you could not go to Skopje city hospital and speak with one of the injured persons who had been detained by the police at or near Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about myself personally, me, as a uniformed police officer, I'm not to go to the hospital. This is done by the police officers from the police station. This is why one of the members was one of the heads of the police stations. This question should be referred to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So the members of the police station could go because they were not in uniform? Is that why they could go to Skopje city hospital?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether they were in uniforms and who were those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you have gone to the Skopje city hospital as a private citizen and asked to speak to one of the -- one or more of the persons who were originally detained by the police in or near Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally thought, and I still think, that it is inappropriate for me to go and do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. Could both committees, General Galevski -- actually, I want to go back to your last response. You said that you think it is inappropriate for you to go and do that. Could you have done it? Could you have gone to Skopje city hospital and tried to speak with one of the persons who been detained?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that then I would interfere with the competences of my colleagues of the criminal police. Therefore, I think that I was neither supposed to nor would even think about going and do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could both of the committees investigating the events in Ljuboten in 2001 have spoken with police personnel who participated in those events?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say what was the number of the police officers in the check-points around Ljuboten and what would it mean to talk to them. Therefore, as a committee, as a commission, especially me as a head of the uniformed police, had available my 30-something colleagues from the headquarters or the staff that I was heading as well as my colleague Ljupco Bliznakovski who was in charge of the city of Skopje. And it was the -- it would be inappropriate to call people that you have no information about at all or indications that some of them was participating specifically. If some name or last name would have been referred to me, then we would be able to discuss things about -- about the things that you are referring to. Unfortunately, no one never -- no one ever indicated a name of a person abusing authority on the field anywhere as well as in Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Galevski, could both committees have gone to Skopje city hospital and reviewed the medical records of Ljuboten residents who were brought from police custody to the hospital following the events on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since you insist, I will once again respond to you more specifically. That -- the methodology is established in our country how is done and that would be done by the head of the homicide department, this is Mr. Besini Ramicevic, upon an order of his head, Zivko Petrovski, who is the head of the criminal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If the methodology of the ministry is not producing adequate results, who has the responsibility to ensure that the methodology is changed?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very broad question. And I think that for the specific case it is the public prosecutor who has the authority to do something because he was there from the very first moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Galevski, I'm not asking you anything about the public prosecutor. I'm asking you about the Ministry of the Interior of Macedonian. My question is: If the methodology, systems in place, set up in place for the ministry, the members of the ministry to do its work, if they're not functioning very well, who would have the responsibility and the authority to change that methodology?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the operational affairs, the one most competent is the director of the bureau for security, public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who does the director of public security report to?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. General, could both committees have reviewed the autopsy report of Mr. Atulla Qaili who was healthy on the 12th of August, 2001, before he was detained by the police, members of the police in Ljuboten and then died the next day in Skopje city hospital? Could they have reviewed the autopsy report that was prepared at the institute for forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think that the colleague that I mentioned previously, the head of the homicide department, had done it or was supposed to do it. That is his work ex officio to be informed about these kind of events. If there is a violent death he is obliged to review all the documents that are originating from the forensic medicine institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And certainly this head of the homicide unit could have done this?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that he could, he had to do it. He was supposed to do it, and I believe that he has done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me, if the results of that autopsy report indicated that the man, Atulla Qaili, had been beaten to death, would that information have changed the opinion in the report that your committee issued?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not informed about this -- the existence of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, can you take my word for it. Suppose such a document exists with that information, would that information have possibly changed the opinion in the report that your committee issued?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to speculate, because I've never seen such an information, nor I know that that information has reached the ministry nor that any of my colleagues have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. My colleague earlier today asked you about the testimony of a witness who's known as M-083. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think given the fact that through the -- in addition to the pseudonym, also his position was mentioned. I think that it would be good do redact this part from the transcript that is available to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Ms. Residovic for that. She's absolutely right. And perhaps we could move into private session for a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It is necessary to break now for the tapes. We resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, earlier today I had asked you some questions about the units of the Ministry of Interior and the army that were involved in the fighting in Aracinovo. Can you recall, General, which units of the police, of the ministry, were involved in that fighting?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this. The [indiscernible] Vicinity of the check-points had army forces and police forces, regular police forces deployed. While in the days when there was direct action in the village on the basis of a previously prepared plan, the village of Aracinovo was divided into two sections viewed from Skopje towards the direction of Kumanovo the main or the central street as considered the axis, the middle of the village. To the left were the army forces and to the right the police forces, who were composed of the posebna unit and the Special Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I've asked you a couple of times, General, whether it would have been helpful if the committee that you served on in August and September 2001 had received information from persons who participated in the operation in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001. Do you think it also might have been helpful if the committee had received information from the persons who planned the operation in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, no action was planned in Ljuboten. I said that at the very beginning, if I remember well. And if there had been any activity of the police forces that were deployed there previously in order to maintain law and order in that region and to control the movements, an action could be carried out only upon -- they were -- upon a provocation by the terrorist gangs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday at page 3768 you explained that Minister Boskoski at no time would skip over you or interrupt or interfere with the chain of command that existed within the Ministry of Interior. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the court usher, please, I would like to show General Galevski again the statement that you gave to the ICTY on the 2nd of December, 2003. And we have copies for the General, the Chamber, and the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, could you turn to the first page, please. No, just the cover page. Do you see your signature there, at the bottom of that cover page?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see my signature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn to what is page 8, please. Page 8 has an item on it called witness acknowledgment. Do you see that? Do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is written in the English and my signature is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you see that your initials are on the bottom of each of the other pages?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, could the interpreters ask him to speak up. We have really difficulties understanding whether it is in the positive or in the -- in the affirmative or in the negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Galevski, you've been asked by the interpreters to please speak a bit more loudly so they can follow you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see that your initials are on each page; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to paragraph 40 of this statement. It is the very last paragraph. Are you at paragraph 40, General?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 40 says this: "Minister Boskoski did not always respect the chain of command, however, but concerning the crisis areas I was always consulted and informed about what was going on but I was never informed that he would have made some personnel changes or when he would have purchased something for the needs of the ministry. These are the things I think he did wrong." Do you see that? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, how do you reconcile what you told the Office of the Prosecutor in December 2003 and what you told the Judges yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to have this in Macedonian -- you to have this in Macedonian and if would you read it better, you would see that everything that has been taken as activity related to the crisis areas, I have always been consulted, not always as far as some personnel issues are concerned which I can -- I'm still confirming and not on all cases, only in certain cases. I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you have the Macedonian version in front of you. That's what I wanted you to read. Do you have paragraph 40 of the Macedonian version in front of you, General?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it, and I do not agree how it states here. It should state "sometimes," not "never."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "Minister Boskoski did not always respect the chain of command." Right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now, how do you reconcile, now that we've done that, how do you reconcile what you've told the ICTY in 2003 to what you told the Judges yesterday, that at no time did Minister Boskoski interrupt or go around the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what you said. I would clarify, we should have a question as it has been asked while in the second sentence it says: "As far as a crisis regions are concerned, I have always been consulted." Therefore, as far as police work is concerned, and police functioning concerned, I stand behind what you said. I was not always consulted about the logistic affairs which are not under my competence. We have a unit for joint affairs which is competent for these things and probably the minister consults with a deputy minister in charge of these kind of affairs, and he didn't have to consult me on that matter. This is why I gave such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So there were times when Minister Boskoski skipped over you within the chain of command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat again. It does not relate to taking professional activities. It relates to some other marginal affairs. He sometimes, for instance, went to -- to a ground without me knowing that. This is what my statement referred to. And I consider that it was okay if the minister was accompanied by the head of the uniformed police to go on the ground and this is what he did sometimes, he went to the ground without being accompanied in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like the usher's assistance, please, to show General Galevski his statement from December 2004, please. We have copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could take a look, please, at the Macedonian version, General, and if you could turn to what is paragraph 21. Are you at paragraph 21 now, General Galevski?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It should have ERN N000-9945 at the top, paragraph marked as 2-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you looking at the statement from December 2004?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the one, but the number you are stating, 21, as you said, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I need to look at the Macedonian copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you -- we could do it another way, General. Can you look at the penultimate paragraph and it begins at the bottom of page 5 in your version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you give that to the General, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, it's paragraph 21 in the English version. It begins with the words: "As far as I know." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "As far as I know, at least until the fall of 2002, there were no other bodies set up to investigate the events in Ljuboten." And then it says this: "On the other hand, I must admit that the then minister of the interior, Mr. Ljube Boskoski, often took decisions and established some Working Groups or similar without keeping his subordinates informed about this." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall, please, General, whether Minister Boskoski took any decisions related to the events in Ljuboten, for example, after the mine incident that killed eight Macedonian soldiers at Ljubotenski Bacila on Friday, the 10th of August? Did the minister of the interior make any decisions after that about what to do, what should be done?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. How about on the next day -- let me actually go back further. On that Friday, the 10th of August, after the mine explosion that killed eight Macedonian soldiers at Ljubotenski Bacila, did the members of the collegium meet from the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say what meetings were held. I know that in the afternoon hours we had an announcement of problems arising in Radusa. I was there on Friday. We were trying to make a shift of the people, and in order to prepare on Saturday this team, to make the shift then with the minister, we took on a alternative route to Radusa to take certain activities. Therefore, as far as Ljuboten was concerned, I don't think there were some special activities on our side. If there had been such activities I believe I would have been informed or at least maybe I have forgotten them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is it your testimony today that after eight Macedonian soldiers are blown up on the -- on Friday morning, the 10th of August, that there were no special activities planned in response by the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Interior has never worked on the retaliation principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, why do you suggest that I was thinking about retaliation? I didn't ask you that.

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exact you do not ask me about you asked me what we planned. We never planned any counteractivities if we were faced with such a loss of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's not the question, though, that I asked you. My question was: What activities of any kind did the members of the Ministry of Interior decide upon, plan upon, after members of the ministry received the news about the killings on the 10th of August?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat: The Ministry of Interior did not plan any activities in the area of Ljuboten, with the exception of regular activities related to the -- to our presence at the check-points around the village just like around Skopje, Tetovo and Kumanovo. There were no special activities planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, you have explained to us, though, that sometimes the minister, Mr. Boskoski, sometimes he made decisions without consulting you. So how can you be sure that there were no such plans?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is misleading the witness to say something that he didn't say. He said that the minister consulted him concerning activities related to his field of work and that he wasn't consulted about some personnel issues and other marginal issues. To say that something that the witness didn't say is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Saxon will direct his question accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll put my question a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is it possible that Minister Boskoski made some decisions on the 10th or 11th of August without consulting you?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he wouldn't do that. I will repeat again. As far as -- I will repeat this. Refers to issues concerning the crisis areas, he would certainly not undertake any steps without informing me about that. If I was unavailable, then some of my colleagues would have called and someone was to be given that task. This is why I certify that there must have been consultation. I said before where the exceptions could have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Minister Boskoski accompany you to the Radusa area on the 11th of August?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So does that mean that you and the minister were together for an entire day, into the evening?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long exactly we were together. I know that long -- most of the day he was there. In the evening he left earlier and I stayed until after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, during that time-period, most of the day when you and Mr. Boskoski were together, was there any discussion about events occurring in or around Ljuboten village?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had fights in Radusa. We did not have time to discuss what was going on in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. General, at pages 3769 through 3770 of the transcript, you described yesterday how after the events in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001, Minister Boskoski had a meeting with Ambassador Ungaro, the OSCE representative. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was precisely like that. 12th of August, if it was Sunday, then I was on a trip and it is on Sunday that the events occurred in Ljuboten that we are discussing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, it may have been my mistake. You described how after the events in Ljuboten there was a meeting between Ambassador Ungaro and Mr. Boskoski. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not only with Ambassador Ungaro but with many other important ambassadors in Skopje. I don't exactly remember the schedule of the meetings, the time of the meetings. I only that he had intense meetings with several ambassadors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you explained how after that meeting with Ambassador Ungaro Minister Boskoski stated publicly that everything that took place in Ljuboten must be investigated. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. But knowing the situation I think this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness a video-clip that is Exhibit P00362.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, this is a video that you'll see that was made very shortly after the meeting with Ambassador Ungaro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you heard what -- the comments of Minister Boskoski and I have a question for you. Did the comments of Minister Boskoski that a massacre did not occur in the village of Ljuboten and that there was no killing of civilians but of a terrorist extremist group, did those comments have any influence on the investigations of the committee that you worked on to review the conduct of the forces of the Ministry of the Interior in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I hear this statement. Probably at that time I was busy with other activities, but listening to the minister's statement now, I think that he said very clearly that it is necessary to make an on-site investigation by independent institutions, the prosecutor and an investigating judge, in order to confirm or to deny --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, we've heard what Minister Boskoski said. I need to stop you because you're not answering my question. My question was simply this. My question was: Did the fact that the minister made public statements to the effect that the persons who were deceased in Ljuboten were members of terrorist groups, did that have any influence on the work of your committee?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this is an unfair question because the witness clearly said that this is the first time that he hears this is interview given by the Minister Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you give an answer to my question, General?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me personally, even when -- if I would have heard this statement, that would have no influence because I know myself, how I've been working for my entire life and how professionally I carry out my duties, no statement neither by the minister nor by any other else would have any impact on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You explained yesterday, General, at page 3769 of the transcript that shortly after the events in Ljuboten you spoke with General Lange, a NATO general, about the possibility of obtaining NATO support so that an on-site investigation could be carried out in Ljuboten. Do you recall explaining that?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not only with him, but also with the others that I had contact with, with the members of the international community. But I remember this person very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And General Lange told you that due to the security situation in Ljuboten village and the signing of the Ohrid agreement. It wasn't advisable for an investigation team to enter Ljuboten, right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He suggested that it would be not a good assessment to go to the village in order to avoid a bigger incident from occurring.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: After the events in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, what would have been more difficult? Performing an on-site investigation in Ljuboten village, or speaking with employees of the Ministry of the Interior who participated in the events in and around Ljuboten on the 12th of August? What would have been more difficult, do you think?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it would be easier to discuss with the employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. On Tuesday you discussed the -- with my learned colleague you discussed the formation of the rapid intervention unit, also known as the Lions, and do you recall who the first commander of the Lions was?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was Goran Stojkov.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was Goran Stojkov's job before he was appointed commander of the Lions?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an employee of the ministry, in the sector for securing persons and facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does that mean he was a security guard or a body-guard?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly his position was, but I know that he worked in this department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But if he is working in that department for security, his job would be to provide security for officials or for buildings. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What qualifications did Goran Stojkov have for becoming commander of the brigade eventually known as the Lions?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he has a higher education, but I would not like to -- I couldn't confirm it for sure because I have talked with Goran on this topic, he has undergone some other training, seminars, courses, but I could not respond to your question more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say that Goran Stojkov had a higher education, are you referring to high school, secondary school?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm -- I think that he is a graduated lawyer. That is at least what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Did he get any education in criminal justice or police studies?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the faculty of law is not within police studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stojkov get any education in security studies?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm, but when he was admitted in that service, I -- surely one of the conditions to be employed at the service would be to have such a qualification, which wasn't up to me, and I could not confirm about it. That is the logical sense of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That would be logical, but you can't confirm it, right?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to becoming the commander of the Lions brigade, Goran Stojkov had never led police units, had he?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Had Goran Stojkov, prior to becoming the commander of the Lions, led any units in combat during the crisis in 2001?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think Goran, since he became a commander of that unit, the only -- only activities that they have in their bases were just exercise activities. They never went in the field where the crisis regions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Galevski, I'm talking about before Goran Stojkov became commander, I want to know what his experience was. So my question is: Before Goran Stojkov was appointed commander of the Lions unit, had he led any units in combat or counterterrorism activities?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I responded to your question. I don't know when exactly he was reassigned to this position from the security administration. Before that, he never participated in the combat activities. At least I'm not aware of that, and I think no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you know, why, then, was Mr. Stojkov appointed to be the commander of this very special unit?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he has some military experience before his time in the police, but I'm not sure. But I think that -- there's something in my mind. I think that he has some kind of an army/military experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: 90 per cent of the men in Macedonia perform their military service. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But as far as I know, Goran had undergone some training in the special army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. Was there a particular event, particular attack perhaps, on Minister Boskoski that led to the start of the Lions unit?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you know, was there a particular event, a particular attack by members of the NLA on Minister Boskoski that led to the start of the Lion unit?

utterances.speaker: RISTO GALEVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on two or three occasions there had been some such attacks. While moving on the Tetovo-Skopje highway I remember well about it. But that was the smallest reason to establish the Lions unit. The Lions unit was established by a decision of the bodies, by the decision of the president and of the government of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take note of the time. I believe I need another ten or 15 minutes with this witness. I will still be under my two-hour time-limit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you in a position to complete that questioning now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I can try, Your Honour, if you will give me that time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can certainly get 10 or 12 minutes on the tape. Or would you prefer that it be tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would prefer that it be tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't be sure of finishing your time on the present tape, so the more practical course would appear to be, then, to adjourn now. We resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 20th day of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
